bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 16: Flat clustering
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, April 1 2009 draft)

question: How can a document collection be partitioned into coherent flat clusters without labels, how is cluster quality measured, and how do K-means and EM work?
hypothesis: Cluster hypothesis: documents in the same cluster behave similarly with respect to relevance to information needs.
contributions: Problem statement for hard flat clustering
Four external evaluation criteria: purity, NMI, Rand index, F measure
K-means with convergence proof, complexity and choice of K (knee, penalty, AIC)
EM for a Bernoulli mixture as soft model-based clustering

limits: Edition is 2008/2009: clustering is of sparse tf-idf vectors with Euclidean or cosine distance; no dense neural embeddings, no k-means++ (only cites Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2006 on worst-case complexity), no mini-batch or spectral or density methods.
Evaluation numbers are one toy example (17 points) and one 1203-document Reuters-RCV1 subset curve; no benchmark comparison of algorithms.
Authors concede the AIC derivation assumes i.i.d. data, only approximately true for text, so AIC (lambda=2M) can rarely be applied unmodified (p.367).
Authors state no consensus that cluster-based retrieval works across scenarios (p.372).
Chapter covers only classical unsupervised clustering; prior-knowledge and interactive clustering are only pointed to (p.374).
Chapter shows the NMI value 0.36 for Figure 16.4 only in Table 16.2 with no worked derivation; the adjusted Rand index is only mentioned in Section 16.6, not defined here.
Figure 2D illustrations may mislead for length-normalised vectors (footnote 2, p.357).
practices: Evaluate a clustering with an external criterion against a gold standard where one exists, and prefer direct task evaluation when affordable (p.356).
Do not use purity or raw mutual information to compare clusterings with different K; use NMI (p.357-358).
Use Rand index for equal weighting of FP and FN, and F with beta>1 when separating similar documents is worse (p.359).
Length-normalise document vectors for K-means in IR (Fig 16.5, p.361).
Combine an RSS or RSS-decrease threshold with a bound on iterations to guarantee termination (p.361-363).
Break ties consistently (lowest index) to avoid cycling (p.363).
Seed K-means by excluding outliers, trying multiple starts and keeping lowest RSS, or seeding from hierarchical clustering on a sample of size iK (p.364).
Estimate K by running i=10 clusterings per K, taking min RSS, and looking for the knee; still apply an external constraint (p.365).
Prefer RSS + lambda*K over AIC for text; choose lambda from past similar datasets (p.367-368).
Initialise EM from a hard K-means clustering, since EM is prone to local optima (p.372).
Truncate centroids or use K-medoids for efficient centroid-document similarity (p.365).

terms.definition: Documents in the same cluster behave similarly with respect to relevance to information needs.
Each document is a member of exactly one cluster.
A document's assignment is a distribution over all clusters.
Each cluster is assigned to its most frequent class; accuracy of this assignment, counting correct documents and dividing by N: (1/N) sum_k max_j |w_k ∩ c_j|.
The percentage of pairwise decisions that are correct: (TP+TN)/(TP+FP+FN+TN), i.e. accuracy over N(N-1)/2 pairs.
F_beta = (beta^2+1)PR/(beta^2 P+R) over pairwise decisions with P=TP/(TP+FP), R=TP/(TP+FN).
Squared distance of each vector from its centroid, summed over all vectors; the K-means objective.
mu(w) = (1/|w|) sum_{x in w} x, the mean of the documents in a cluster.
The document vector closest to the centroid.
A measure of how much documents deviate from the prototype of their clusters (e.g. RSS for K-means).
K = argmin [-2L(K) + 2q(K)]; for K-means, K = argmin [RSS_min(K) + 2MK].
Assumes the data were generated by a model and tries to recover the original model from the data.
Iterative maximisation of L(D|Theta), alternating an expectation step (soft assignment) and a maximization step (parameters).

problems: Table 16.3 and Figures 16.4/16.6/16.7 are flattened by the text layer: Table 16.3 rows show 7 values against 8 iteration columns (0,1,2,3,4,5,15,25) so column alignment cannot be recovered from the text; only values quoted in prose were used.
Figures are images; Fig 16.8 values read only qualitatively.
Inconsistency: F5 for Figure 16.4 printed 0.46 in Table 16.2 and 0.456 in text p.360.

Inconsistency: Section 16.2 says 'We define clustering to be exhaustive' but K-means text allows singleton and empty clusters; not a contradiction but empty clusters violate the surjectivity demand of Section 16.2.
Inconsistency: Exercise 16.5 cites 'page 361' for termination conditions; they appear on pp.361-363. Minor.
